pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Magnetic Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** England DfE KS2 Year 3 'Forces and magnets' — 'compare and group together a variety of everyday materials on the basis of whether they are attracted to a magnet, and identify some magnetic materials' and 'observe how magnets attract or repel each other and attract some materials and not others';

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NGSS 3-PS2-3 (ask questions about cause-and-effect of magnetic interactions between objects not in contact; DCI PS2.B).

- **Operational details:** Best practice combines EXPLICIT teaching with many counter-examples and a structured practical, because the headline misconception is unusually robust and is even held by teachers.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 7-8). The goal is an empirical, testable property — which materials a magnet attracts, and that two magnets both attract AND repel — discovered by hands-on predict-test-record-conclude, NOT any model of fields or domains (reserve that for KS3).
bestPractices: Run a predict-test-record-conclude practical: child predicts for each object, then tests with a magnet, records the result, and concludes what the magnetic ones have in common (iron/steel/nickel/cobalt).

Deliberately stock the object set with CONFOUND counter-examples — copper coin, aluminium ring, brass key, gold/silver-coloured non-ferrous items — so 'all metals' and 'all shiny things' are visibly disproved in the child's own hand.

Teach explicitly, with many examples, that only some metals are magnetic (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt and their alloys); most metals (copper, aluminium, gold, silver) are not — don't rely on discovery alone.
Separate two distinct ideas: being ATTRACTED to a magnet (a magnetic material) is not the same as BEING a magnet — test by flipping the magnet; a true magnet will then be repelled.

Give first-hand experience of BOTH attraction and repulsion between two magnets, including the invisible 'push' of repulsion, and repeat tests so the response is felt as a stable property of the material.
Pre-empt cross-topic confusion: keep magnetism distinct from static electricity (test a charged balloon) and from gravity (it is not 'the Earth being a giant magnet').
keyRepresentations: A sorting tray / two-column record: magnetic vs non-magnetic, populated by real testing
A mixed object set chosen to break the rule: paperclip & steel scissors (attract) beside copper coin, aluminium ring, brass key, plastic, wood (don't)
Two bar magnets brought together to show attract, then one flipped to show repel
A simple 'is it a magnet?' flip-test: if it's repelled when the magnet is turned round, it is itself a magnet
commonMisconceptions: 'All metals are magnetic / magnets stick to any metal' — THE robust misconception, reinforced by earlier conductor/insulator (metals-are-special) teaching, and frequently held by teachers themselves (IOP Spark; NSTA).
'Anything shiny or silver-coloured is magnetic' — the same error generalised by appearance rather than material.
Confusing 'attracted to a magnet' with 'is a magnet'.
'Bigger magnet = stronger magnet' — strength depends on material, not just size (IOP Spark).
Merging magnetism with static electricity or with gravity (both act at a distance, so children conflate them).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, learners investigate that only some materials (iron, most steels, nickel, cobalt and many alloys containing them) are attracted to magnets — NOT all metals and NOT all shiny things — through a predict-test-record-conclude cycle with deliberately chosen counter-examples, including shiny non-ferrous metals so shininess and metal-ness are held constant. A second strand gives first-hand experience of both attraction AND repulsion between two magnets, and separates 'attracted to a magnet' from 'being a magnet' via a flip-test. The goal is an empirical, testable property discovered by hands-on investigation, not any model of fields or domains (reserve that for later).

activities.title: Predict–test–record–conclude with a confound-rich object set
feedback: If the learner predicts 'all of them, they're metal', let them test the solid copper item, aluminium ring and brass key (pre-checked as non-magnetic) — watch these non-ferrous metals stay unmoved while the steel leaps to the magnet; this is the disconfirming moment.

If the learner sorts by appearance ('shiny things stick'), use the three shiny items: all three are shiny and all are metal, yet only the shiny steel is attracted (as long as the copper item is solid copper, not copper-plated steel), so appearance is visibly ruled out; then add the dull rusty iron nail (attracted) to show dullness does not prevent it either.
When the sort is complete, prompt: 'What is the SAME about everything in the magnetic column?' to move from listing results to naming the material.

Reinforce explicitly: only some metals are magnetic — iron, most steels, nickel, cobalt and many alloys containing them (some stainless steels are not); copper, aluminium, gold and silver are not — don't rely on the child inferring the full rule from discovery alone.
activities.rationale: 'All metals are magnetic' is a documented, robust misconception, partly transferred from earlier conductor/insulator teaching where metals are treated as special. Predicting then watching counter-examples fail in one's own hand is intended to provide the disconfirming experience the belief needs, and holding shininess and metal-ness constant across three shiny items rules those out as the cause and points to the material; explicit naming of the magnetic materials supplies what discovery alone may miss.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: compare and group materials by whether attracted to a magnet and identify some magnetic materials; observe how magnets attract or repel each other and attract some materials and not others.

'All metals are magnetic' is a documented, research-backed misconception partly transferred from primary conductor/insulator (metals-are-special) teaching; paired with 'size of magnet dictates its strength'.
KS2 Y3 lesson names the target misconception as 'all metals and silver-coloured objects are magnetic' and addresses it with explicit teaching plus hands-on exploration.
Not all metals are attracted (copper, aluminium, gold, silver are not); iron/steel/nickel/cobalt and their alloys are; being attracted is not the same as being a magnet (flip-test reveals it).
learnerActions: Lay out a mixed set of everyday objects chosen to break the rule: a steel paperclip and steel scissors (attract), beside a solid copper item (e.g. a short piece of copper pipe or wire), an aluminium can-ring/tab, a solid brass key, a plastic brick and a wooden block (don't). The adult should check each item with a magnet beforehand: many 'copper' coins (e.g. UK 1p/2p from 1992 onwards, euro 1–5 cent coins) are copper-plated steel and DO stick, and some keys are steel.
Before testing, predict for EACH object whether a magnet will stick to it, and say WHY.

Include three SHINY items together — a shiny steel paperclip, a shiny solid copper item (pre-checked; not a copper-plated steel coin) and a shiny aluminium tab — so that all three are shiny and all are metal, and the difference that matters is the material they are made of.
Bring a magnet to each object in turn and observe whether it is attracted or not.
Record each result in two columns: magnetic vs non-magnetic.
Look at the magnetic column and conclude what those objects have in common — they are iron/steel (and, when named, nickel/cobalt).
Repeat with a dull, rusty iron nail alongside a shiny solid copper item (pre-checked as non-magnetic) to check whether shininess predicts attraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Magnets attract specific materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt), not metals-in-general and not shiny/silver-coloured things. The deciding factor is what the material actually is, not whether it is a metal or whether it looks shiny.

activities.title: Feel both attraction and repulsion between two magnets
feedback: If the learner expects magnets to only ever pull, draw attention to the moment the flipped magnet pushes back before contact — the invisible push is the key new experience.
If a result seems random, have them repeat the same orientation to confirm it behaves the same way every time.

If the learner assumes a larger magnet must automatically be stronger, note that bigger does not automatically mean stronger — strength depends on the material and how it is magnetised, not size alone.
activities.rationale: Repeated first-hand testing helps children internalise that the interaction is a stable property that repeats, and feeling repulsion (not just attraction) addresses the curriculum requirement to observe how magnets both attract and repel.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: compare and group materials by whether attracted to a magnet and identify some magnetic materials; observe how magnets attract or repel each other and attract some materials and not others.

Repeated first-hand testing helps children internalise that each material reacts the same way every time (a stable property); the 'magnets attract all metals' misconception is common among teachers too.
learnerActions: Bring two bar magnets together one way and feel them snap together (attract).
Flip one magnet end-for-end and bring the SAME two magnets together again — feel them push apart (repel), including the invisible 'push' before they touch.
Repeat the attract-then-flip-to-repel test several times so the response is felt as a stable, repeatable property.
Describe in your own words that two magnets can BOTH attract and repel depending on which ends face each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Attraction and repulsion are two faces of one magnetic force between magnets; a magnet can push as well as pull, and which happens depends on which poles face each other (orientation), not chance.

activities.title: Flip-test: 'attracted to a magnet' vs 'is a magnet'
feedback: If the learner calls the attracted paperclip 'a magnet', run the flip-test: the paperclip is attracted both ways and never repels, so it is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
Use the second bar magnet as the contrast case so the learner sees what repulsion-on-flip actually looks like.
Prompt the transfer question: 'If I gave you a brand-new metal, how would you find out whether it's magnetic?' to check they reach for testing rather than appearance.
activities.rationale: Conflating 'attracted to a magnet' with 'is a magnet' is a specific documented confusion; the flip/repulsion test gives learners an operational way to tell them apart.
sourceClaims: Not all metals are attracted (copper, aluminium, gold, silver are not); iron/steel/nickel/cobalt and their alloys are; being attracted is not the same as being a magnet (flip-test reveals it).
learnerActions: Stick a paperclip to a magnet and notice it is attracted.
Ask: is the paperclip itself now a magnet? Decide how to check.
Turn the magnet around (so the opposite pole faces the paperclip) and bring it to the paperclip again — observe that the paperclip is still attracted, never repelled.
Contrast with a known second magnet, which IS repelled when a like pole is turned toward it.
Conclude that something attracted to a magnet is a magnetic material, but a true magnet is the thing that can also repel when turned around.
activities.intendedInsight: Being attracted to a magnet (a magnetic material) is not the same as being a magnet. The distinguishing test is repulsion: a magnetic material is attracted whichever way the magnet faces, while only another magnet can be made to push away when a like pole is turned toward it.

activities.title: Keep magnetism distinct from static electricity and gravity
feedback: If the learner says a magnet attracts paper or plastic like the balloon does, re-run the object sort — magnets leave paper and plastic unmoved.
If the learner treats gravity as 'the Earth being a giant magnet', point out gravity pulls wood and plastic down too, which magnets never attract.
activities.rationale: Children commonly conflate magnetism with static electricity and gravity because all act at a distance; a brief explicit contrast pre-empts this cross-topic confusion.
learnerActions: Rub a balloon to charge it and see it attract small bits of paper or hair; compare this with how a magnet behaves toward the sorted objects.

Discuss that although both a charged balloon and a magnet can act without touching, a magnet only attracts iron/steel-type materials while the charged balloon attracts light bits of many different materials.
State that magnetism is a property of certain materials, separate from gravity, which pulls everything down regardless of material.
activities.intendedInsight: Magnetism, static electricity and gravity are different forces; acting at a distance is something they share, but they are not the same thing and should not be merged.

constraints: Keep the work at a concrete, observational level for ages 7–8: investigate which materials a magnet attracts and that two magnets both attract and repel. Do NOT introduce magnetic fields or domains at this stage.

The object set must include confounding counter-examples (copper, aluminium, brass, and shiny/silver-coloured non-ferrous items) and at least one shiny magnetic item, or the 'all metals' and 'all shiny things' beliefs cannot be visibly disproved.

A hands-on physical kit matters here: the felt pull of a magnet, and especially the invisible push of repulsion, is a physical force/haptic sensation that on-screen artefacts cannot output, so a physical kit should accompany any screen work rather than be replaced by it. The on-screen bench can still support the cognitive 'which materials / why' goal.

An on-screen test-bench (predict-toggle per object, auto-sorting magnetic vs non-magnetic columns, a two-magnet zone where flipping a pole switches snap-together to push-apart) can support the 'which materials / why' goal and serve many counter-examples quickly, but should accompany, not replace, physical testing. This is one option, not the only way to teach it.

A labelled tap-to-reveal scene (tap an object → magnetic or not; lift-the-flap 'is it a magnet or just magnetic?') is a useful consolidation and naming reference, but nothing is predicted or felt to fail, so it should follow the disconfirming investigation rather than lead it.

Drag-to-sort categorisation, prediction multiple-choice with shiny-metal distractors, and 'magnet vs magnetic material' items check and consolidate understanding and make good retrieval/assessment, but on their own they do not elicit the first-hand 'rule fails' experience.

Explicit teaching with many examples should accompany discovery: name iron, most steels, nickel, cobalt and many alloys containing them as magnetic (some stainless steels are not) and copper, aluminium, gold, silver as not — do not rely on the child inferring the complete rule unaided.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording ('intended to') reflects this.
Several sources in the original row are marked verified:false (Oak National Academy, TESSA/Open University, NSTA) and their claims should be checked before being relied upon.

The original row asserted that live on-screen recompute 'is what breaks the misconception, which a static picture cannot do' and that a static image 'cannot do the disconfirming work'. These are catalog preferences, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements (a fixed scene does not let the learner predict-and-watch-fail, but can still teach as reference/consolidation).

The original categorical claims that 3D rendering 'adds nothing' and that a conversation format 'cannot help / is not built by dialogue' were removed as impermissible categorical modality claims. The narrow observations behind them are set aside rather than endorsed: because the phenomenon is a flat sort-by-material-property, 3D depth/viewpoint offers no extra discrimination; and because the learners are early readers, dialogue is a weak primary vehicle. Neither is treated as a universal law or as proof of medium superiority.

The 'bigger magnet = stronger magnet' misconception is retained conservatively as a feedback aside; the row attributes 'strength depends on material, not size' to IOP Spark, which is plausible but was not re-verified here. The feedback is phrased so that strength depends on material and magnetisation, not size alone (it does not claim size is irrelevant).

assess.poeTask: Lay out a copper coin, an aluminium can-tab, a steel paperclip and a brass screw. Ask the child to predict which the magnet will lift and WHY before testing. Predicting 'all of them, they're metal' is the diagnostic tell; watching only the steel lift breaks the all-metals rule.
probeDeeper: Here's a dull, rusty iron nail and a shiny copper coin — which will the magnet pull, and why?
The paperclip stuck to the magnet. Is the paperclip now a magnet itself? How could we check?
If I gave you a brand-new metal you'd never seen, how would you find out whether it's magnetic?
assess.correctAnswer: Only the steel paperclip is pulled. Magnets attract iron and steel (and nickel and cobalt), not other metals like copper or aluminium — so it isn't shininess or 'being a metal' that matters, but what the material actually is.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All metals are magnetic — the magnet will pull all three because they're metal.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test copper, aluminium and brass as counter-examples in a predict-test-record-conclude cycle; name iron, steel, nickel and cobalt as the magnetic ones.
errorPatterns.distractor: The magnet will pull all three, because they are all metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts copper and aluminium are attracted too.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair a dull, rusty iron nail (attracted) with a shiny aluminium tab (not) to break the shininess rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts by appearance — predicts a shiny non-ferrous item attracted and a dull iron item not.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'If something is attracted to a magnet, then it IS a magnet.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Flip-test: a real magnet is REPELLED when turned around, but the paperclip never repels — so it isn't a magnet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the paperclip 'a magnet' after it sticks.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts by 'metal' or 'shiny' — expects all metals or all shiny things to be pulled; may call an attracted object a magnet.
responseLevels.full: Explains that magnets attract specific materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt), not metals-in-general or shiny things, predicts a novel object correctly, and distinguishes 'attracted to a magnet' from 'is a magnet' using the repulsion test.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly picks the steel paperclip after testing and knows some things are attracted and some aren't, but explains it as 'metal' or 'shiny', or just lists what stuck, without naming that only iron/steel-type materials are magnetic — can't yet predict a new material.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I have a shiny copper coin, a shiny steel paperclip, and a shiny aluminium can-tab. I hold a magnet near each one. Which will the magnet pull and which won't — and what makes the difference between them?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: All three items are shiny metals, so a child who thinks 'all metals are magnetic' or 'shiny/silver things are magnetic' predicts all three pulled. Only a child who knows magnetism attracts specific materials singles out the steel paperclip and, in tier 2, names the material rather than the metal-ness or shine as the cause. Holding shininess and metal-ness constant across the three items is what exposes the belief.
